The rain did not fall so much as it descended, a heavy, gray curtain that erased the horizon line where the sky met the distant hills. It was a relentless, rhythmic drumming against the stone parapets of the old bridge, a structure that had stood for centuries, weathered by countless storms just like this one. The bridge itself was an arch of dark granite, slick and shining under the downpour, reflecting the dim, flickering light of the lanterns that lined its length. These lanterns were not electric, nor were they fueled by modern gas; they held small, trembling flames within glass panes that had been polished by generations of hands. Each flame was a tiny, defiant star against the overwhelming gloom of the wet evening, casting pools of warm, amber light onto the wet cobblestones.

As the wind picked up, swirling the mist around the base of the bridge, the lanterns swayed gently on their iron hooks. The light they cast was not steady; it danced and jittered, creating elongated shadows that stretched across the railing and dipped into the churning water below. The river beneath was swollen with the rain, its surface broken by whitecaps and eddies that rushed past the stone pillars with a low, guttural roar. The sound of the water was a constant, deep thrum that vibrated through the soles of one’s boots, a reminder of the raw power of nature that the bridge sought to tame.

Walking across the bridge in such weather was an exercise in solitude. The world beyond the span of the lanterns’ glow was invisible, swallowed by the gray veil of the rain.
